Appendix 1 (Treasury Portfolio) — referenced at cover §3.8 for the loan-by-loan Q4 detail and at §§3.15-3.16 for investments and non-treasury investments — is NOT on this disk. Treasury-content is thin across the three papers actually read: the cover gives aggregate LT-debt totals and rate; App 2 gives PIs; App 3 is a standing TMP document with no live figures. Officer address published on cover page 1 (iburbidge@swindon.gov.uk). Balance-sheet identity ties at both year-ends (CFR - external borrowing - OLTL = internal borrowing). Email drafted around the dated strategy assumption at cover §3.5 (rates were forecast to fall; they didn't) and the shape of the short book that decision has created.

facts.value: £110m of new long-term borrowing in 2025/26 — 16 loans (15 interest-only maturity, of which 2 for the HRA, plus 1 EIP). New GENERAL FUND loans at average 4.72% and average maturity 1.8 years. HRA loans at average 4.96% and average maturity 10 years.

source.title: Cover paragraph 3.4, page 2

facts.note: The 1.8-year average maturity on new GF borrowing is short. Combined with the strategy statement at 3.5 this is the defining decision of the year — 'shorter maturity dates in the anticipation of securing lower interest rates when they became due for refinancing'. Our own maturity profile at 2026-08-16 shows 16 loans totalling £82.8m in the 0-2y bucket at ~4.4% average, which is where most of these new short GF drawings have landed.

facts.value: "At the beginning of the 25/26 financial year loans were taken out with shorter maturity dates in the anticipation of securing lower interest rates when they became due for refinancing and as interest rates were forecast to fall. However, interest rates have not fallen as quickly as forecast and the strategy is still to take out new loans for shorter periods in the expectation that interest rates do begin to fall, but to also take out some loans over periods up to 7 years to mitigate refinancing risk." (§3.5, page 2)

source.title: Cover paragraph 3.5, page 2

facts.note: The single most falsifiable claim in the paper — and the current strategy re-states it. Bank Rate started 25/26 at 4.50% and ended 25/26 at 3.75% (three -25bp cuts in the first eight months of 25/26, then held). Bank Rate has stayed at 3.75% into August 2026 per the market data we hold. Long PWLB certainty curve is higher today than at year-end: 1y 4.95% (-9bp), 5y 5.34% (+6bp), 10y 5.83% (+11bp), 20y 6.38% (+15bp), 50y 6.27% (+23bp). The dated assumption is the natural hook for the email — read the paper, quote the sentence, show where the curve went.

summary.text:
Swindon Borough Council's Treasury Management Performance 2025/26 (doc 146955) went to Audit Committee on 23 June 2026 (with the same paper in Cabinet's July 2026 work programme). Three papers read from local disk: 7-page cover (146955), 2-page Prudential Indicators (146957) and 29-page Treasury Management Practices for 2026/27 (146958). Appendix 1 (Treasury Portfolio) — which the cover references at §3.8 for the loan-by-loan Q4 detail — is not on this disk. Contact officer is Ian Burbidge (iburbidge@swindon.gov.uk, direct dial published in the running footer of every page). Title is not stated in the paper; Schedule S.6 of the TMP names the Section 151 Officer as the Director of Finance & Audit but does not name the incumbent. Treasury adviser is MUFG Corporate Markets, a recent appointment (contract commenced 1 October 2025).

The loan-book reconciliation does not cleanly tie. Our PWLB file for Swindon at 31/3/26 carries 65 loans totalling £396,520,166 at a principal-weighted 3.5296%; the paper's cover Table 1 prints gross long-term external borrowing of £422.6m (composed of GF £326.1m + HRA £96.5m) with an all-in weighted rate of 3.58% over the year (§3.7). The £26.08m gap is consistent with non-PWLB long-term borrowing — Market (long-term), Local Authorities or Municipal Bond Agency are all approved sources at TMP 4.7 — and the implied non-PWLB weighted rate to reconcile is ≈4.35%. Without Appendix 1 we cannot verify the source split. Per PIPELINE the loan-book claim is kept out of the email entirely.

Balance-sheet identity ties at both year-ends within rounding. Putting PFI back on both sides: 31/3/25 CFR 558.6 − ext 395.5 − OLTL 34.2 = 128.9 vs paper's 128.8 (0.1 rounding); 31/3/26 CFR 572.0 − ext 422.6 − OLTL 30.7 = 118.7 vs paper's 118.7 exactly. Disclosure is internally consistent — the cover excludes PFI from Table 1 for readability (§3.23) but everything reconciles once PFI is put back on both sides.

The defining decision of the year is at cover §3.4-3.5. £110m of new long-term borrowing across 16 loans — 15 interest-only maturity loans (two of them HRA) plus one EIP — was drawn against £82.9m of maturities, taking gross long-term debt from £395.5m to £422.6m. New General Fund loans came in at an average 4.72% with an average maturity of 1.8 years; the two HRA loans at an average 4.96% over 10 years. The strategy at §3.5 is stated explicitly: 'At the beginning of the 25/26 financial year loans were taken out with shorter maturity dates in the anticipation of securing lower interest rates when they became due for refinancing and as interest rates were forecast to fall. However, interest rates have not fallen as quickly as forecast and the strategy is still to take out new loans for shorter periods…'. This is a dated, falsifiable assumption in the council's own paper — Bank Rate started 25/26 at 4.50%, took three 25bp cuts in the first eight months, and has held at 3.75% since December 2025. The long PWLB curve has moved higher since the paper's 31/3/26 reference: 10y +11bp, 20y +15bp, 50y +23bp. Our maturity profile shows £82.8m of the PWLB book inside 2 years at ~4.4% average; the natural comparison is to today's 1y certainty rate of 4.95%.

Balance-sheet story otherwise: whole CFR growth this year is HRA (+£14.0m to £100.5m); GF barely moved (+£2.9m excl PFI, −£0.6m incl PFI as £7.0m MRP and £3.5m PFI amortisation offset £6.4m borrowing-funded GF capex). Internal borrowing fell £10.2m as £27m of new external landed against £16.7m of CFR growth; GF is 26% under-borrowed (§3.24) and HRA moved from zero to £4m under-borrowed for the first time. Investments dropped from £39.6m to £21.6m at year-end; average daily balance £39.1m at 3.59%; investment period ran to just 11 days as cashflow requirements dominated.

The HRA financing-cost ratio moved 30.3% → 35.2% against a 31.0% indicator (App 2 Table 1), reflecting 'lower than expected income in 2025/26 and the higher cost of borrowing than was anticipated'. HRA debt per dwelling rose £8,307 → £9,724 (+17%); HRA reserves cut from £8.6m indicator to £4.1m actual. Real HRA pressure signal — noted for the file but not the primary email hook (touches on advice quickly).

courses_named: Borrowing short against a rate view
Refinancing decisions and the roll of maturity loans
The liability benchmark and internal borrowing
officer.body:
Hi Ian,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, the inter-LA lending market, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Performance 2025/26 report that went to Audit Committee on 23 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is clearly laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The sentence that stood out is your paragraph 3.5: 'At the beginning of the 25/26 financial year loans were taken out with shorter maturity dates in the anticipation of securing lower interest rates when they became due for refinancing and as interest rates were forecast to fall. However, interest rates have not fallen as quickly as forecast…'. That's a dated, testable claim, which is unusual — most outturn reports state what happened without telling you what was expected of the world when the decisions were taken. Bank Rate did fall three times in the first eight months of 25/26 to 3.75%, then held there, and it's still 3.75% now. The long PWLB certainty curve has drifted higher since 31 March — the 10-year is 0.11% higher, the 20-year 0.15%, the 50-year 0.23% — while the 1-year has come off about 0.09%.

Against that, the shape of your short book is the interesting bit. We hold PWLB only, so we can't see the whole picture (your paragraph 3.6 gives total long-term borrowing of £422.6m and the split by source is presumably in Appendix 1 which we don't hold), but our file shows £38m of your PWLB running off inside twelve months at an average 4.56%, and another £44m running off between one and two years at 4.26%. Today's 1-year PWLB certainty rate is 4.95% and the 5-year is 5.34%, so replacing the sub-1-year book at a similar tenor costs about 0.4 points more, and pushing it out to five years costs about 1.1 points more. The current strategy at 3.5 is to keep taking new borrowing shorter, with some 5-7-year loans to spread refinancing risk and some EIP structures — the same bet on rates falling, made a second time. Whether that keeps paying depends on how the next few Monetary Policy Committee meetings go.

The balance sheet ties. Putting PFI back on both sides — CFR £572.0m at 31/3/26 less external borrowing £422.6m less other long-term liabilities £30.7m — gives internal borrowing of £118.7m, which is exactly your 'gross over/under borrowing' figure in Table 1. Your General Fund is 26% under-borrowed (paragraph 3.24), and the HRA has moved from zero to £4m under-borrowed for the first time. Whole CFR growth this year is HRA — £86.5m to £100.5m — with General Fund almost flat once MRP and PFI amortisation are put back in.

One thing worth noting from Appendix 2: your HRA financing-cost ratio moved 30.3% to 35.2% against a 31.0% indicator, and the commentary attributes that to lower income and higher cost of borrowing than assumed when the indicators were set in February 2025. That variance between the indicator set nine months out and the outturn sits alongside the £4m HRA under-borrow — a picture that reads differently now than it would have done at the February setting.

The pages that go with all this: today's rates at both fixings and the whole curve are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard; the monthly picture of what the sector is actually drawing at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity (July 2026 was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%); and pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis prices any PWLB position daily against the DMO's repayment curve.

One standing note. CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates put the liability benchmark in front of every member. Your Appendix 2 gives the CFR and the debt but not a benchmark pathway; ours is fed by live rates so the shape moves as the market does, and it's a useful complement to whatever your adviser currently produces for you.

On training, three of our 115 courses fit what the report describes: Borrowing short against a rate view goes to the strategy at 3.5, Refinancing decisions and the roll of maturity loans covers the £82m running off inside two years, and The liability benchmark and internal borrowing is the natural companion to your Table 1. All courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others — inside Swindon or across to any of the neighbouring authorities — would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
